AirLLM Claims You Can Run a 70B Model on 4GB of VRAM. Here’s What They’re Not Telling You.

Sumit Pandey

The truth behind the viral claim, explained like you’re debugging it over coffee.

Last week, I saw a LinkedIn post that made me do a double-take. Someone was claiming they ran a 70-billion parameter model on a GPU with just 4GB of VRAM. My first reaction? “No way.” My second reaction? “Wait… how?”

If you cant read the article further than please click here

As someone who spent their PhD wrestling with GPU memory limits while training medical imaging models at the University of Copenhagen, I know the pain of staring at CUDA out-of-memory errors at 2 AM. So when AirLLM promises to run a 70B model on hardware that most people use for gaming, I had to dig deeper. And what I found was… complicated.

The Claim Sounds Too Good To Be True

Let’s start with some basic math. A 70B parameter model in full precision (FP16) takes up roughly 140GB of memory. Your GPU has 4GB. That’s like trying to park a Boeing 747 in your living room. So how does AirLLM pull this off?

The answer is surprisingly simple: it doesn’t load the whole model into memory. Instead, it loads the model one layer at a time. Process a layer, throw it out, load the next one. Each layer of a 70B model is roughly 1.6GB, which fits comfortably in 4GB of VRAM.

Think of it like reading a 500-page book, but you can only hold one page at a time. You can read the entire book. It’s just going to take you a while.

To Understand the Catch, You Need to Understand How LLMs Generate Text

Here’s where most articles about AirLLM stop. They show you the magic trick but don’t explain why the rabbit looks a little tired. Let me fix that. LLM text generation happens in two stages. This is important, so stay with me.

  • Stage 1: Prefill. When you send a prompt to an LLM, the model processes all your input tokens in parallel. This stage is compute-bound, meaning it’s limited by how fast your GPU can crunch numbers. GPUs are really good at crunching numbers. So this part is fast. During prefill, the model also builds something called the KV cache (Key-Value cache). Think of it as a cheat sheet. Instead of re-reading your entire prompt every time it generates a new word, the model saves the important bits in this cache.
  • Stage 2: Decoding. This is where the model generates text one token at a time. For each new token, the model needs to look at the entire prompt plus everything it has generated so far. The KV cache saves us from reprocessing old tokens, but here’s the bottleneck: the model weights and KV cache need to move from VRAM to the GPU’s processing cores.

This makes decoding memory-bound. It’s not limited by compute power. It’s limited by how fast data can travel through the GPU’s memory bus.

Here’s the Part That Changes Everything

In the last 20 years of GPU development, compute capacity has grown roughly 60,000x. Memory bandwidth? Only about 100x. Read that again. There’s a 600x gap between how fast GPUs can compute and how fast they can move data around. This is the fundamental bottleneck of modern AI inference.

Now, with standard inference, the data moves from VRAM to GPU cores. That’s already the bottleneck. But with AirLLM’s layer-by-layer approach, we’re adding another, much slower step: moving data from your SSD to VRAM first, and then from VRAM to GPU cores.

SSD-to-VRAM transfer is orders of magnitude slower than VRAM-to-GPU-core transfer. It’s like adding a horse-drawn carriage ride before your Formula 1 race.

So How Slow Are We Talking?

Let me be honest with you. Reports from the community range from about 5 seconds per token with batched prompts to over 100 seconds per token in worst-case scenarios. Some users have reported speeds as slow as one token per minute.

For context, when you use ChatGPT and see text streaming in real-time, that’s happening at roughly 30–50 tokens per second. AirLLM’s layer-by-layer approach turns a real-time conversation into something closer to sending a letter by pigeon.

Then What’s the Point?

Here’s where I push back on the cynics. AirLLM isn’t trying to replace your ChatGPT experience. It’s solving a different problem entirely.

Imagine you’re a student in a country where renting cloud GPUs costs more than your monthly salary. Or you’re a researcher who needs to test how a full-precision 70B model behaves on a specific task, not a quantized approximation of it. Or you’re running offline batch processing where you can kick off a job and come back tomorrow.

For these use cases, AirLLM is genuinely useful. It’s not about speed. It’s about access. A researcher with a $200 GPU can now experiment with the same frontier models that billion-dollar companies use. That matters.

The library also supports some clever optimizations: Flash Attention for efficient memory access, prefetching (loading the next layer while computing the current one), and optional 4-bit/8-bit quantization that can speed things up by roughly 3x.

The Verdict: It Depends on What You’re Looking For

Is AirLLM’s claim accurate? Technically, yes. You can run a 70B model on 4GB of VRAM. The model runs. The outputs are correct. No quantization is required.

But “can run” and “can run usefully” are two very different things. If you need anything resembling real-time inference (chatbots, interactive applications, streaming responses), AirLLM is not your tool. The IO bottleneck from disk-to-VRAM transfer makes it impractical for these use cases.

Here’s my honest take:

  • AirLLM is great for: Offline batch processing, research experimentation, students and hobbyists on a budget, testing full-precision model behavior, and running jobs where latency simply doesn’t matter.
  • AirLLM is not great for: Chatbots, real-time applications, production serving, or anything where a user is waiting for a response.

What This Really Tells Us About the Future

What excites me most about AirLLM isn’t the library itself. It’s what it reveals about the state of AI infrastructure.

The fact that memory bandwidth (not compute) is the real bottleneck tells us where the next breakthroughs need to happen. We don’t need faster math. We need faster highways for data.

Projects like AirLLM, llama.cpp, and others are essentially hacking around a hardware limitation with clever software. But the 600x gap between compute growth and memory bandwidth growth isn’t closing anytime soon. Until chip designers solve the memory wall problem, we’ll keep seeing creative workarounds like this.

And honestly? I think that’s beautiful. Constraints breed creativity. AirLLM might not replace your cloud GPU setup, but it just gave a student somewhere the ability to run a frontier model for the first time. That’s worth celebrating.
